title: Copies and references
summary: Assigning a list or object does not copy it. Learn when two names share one thing, and how to make a real copy.

sections.heading: Two names, one object
body: Writing `b = a` for a list or object does not copy it. Both names now point at the same thing, so a change through one shows up through the other.

javascript.code:
const a = [1, 2]
const b = a
b.push(3)
console.log(a)

sections.heading: Functions receive the same object
body: Passing a list to a function hands over the same list, not a copy. If the function changes it, the caller sees the change.

python.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append('new')

mine = []
add_item(mine)
print(mine)

sections.heading: Shallow and deep copies
body: Spreading (`{ ...obj }`, `[...arr]`) or `.copy()` makes a new outer object, but anything nested inside is still shared. That is a shallow copy.
To copy all the way down, use `structuredClone` in JavaScript or `copy.deepcopy` in Python.

python.code:
import copy

original = {'name': 'Ada', 'tags': ['math']}
shallow = original.copy()
shallow['name'] = 'Bo'
shallow['tags'].append('code')
print(original)

deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
deep['tags'].append('art')
print(original['tags'])

mistakes: `const` stops you reassigning the name, not changing the object it points to.
Changing the input list inside a solution when the task expects a new list.
Expecting a spread copy to protect nested arrays or objects.
